extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor/literary theory; playwrights and comedy writers interested in comic mechanism
extracted.subtask_description: The page is a theoretical analysis of how situational comedy works, identifying archetypal mechanical images and three formal methods (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference) that produce the ludicrous. Useful for critics, dramatists, and anyone designing comic scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatism / mechanical repetition (Jack-in-the-box)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic effect arises when an action, phrase, or exclamation recurs automatically like a machine — a fixed idea expressed by mechanical repetition (e.g., Harpagon’s recurring “No dowry wanted!”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This automatism creates the image of a repeating machine behind a living person; repeated utterances renew and reinforce tension (the 'spring') until release produces laughter. Example: Molière’s use of a repeated regret-sentence; the mechanical recurrence should look habitual and involuntary. Anti-pattern: mere repetition without the sense of underlying fixed idea or escalating tension will not be comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double personality / inner duel
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic scene can be the outward refraction of an inner comedy in which one character contains two opposing impulses (e.g., Alceste the misanthropist vs. the polite gentleman), so the true scene is between the two sides of the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition of a phrase ('I don’t say that!') may reveal escalating internal struggle rather than simple external interaction; laughter comes from seeing a character become angrier with himself as the internal tension renews. The writer should present both aspects (or make their conflict perceptible) so the audience perceives the inner duel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing-jack / manipulated character
rubrics_metrics.description: One character appears to act freely but is, from a certain standpoint, a toy manipulated by another (the 'dancing-jack'), exposing a mechanical arrangement behind apparent freedom (e.g., Scapin manipulating Geronte and Argante).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The spectator can enjoy being complicit (siding with the knave) or simply retain the impression of strings being pulled. To use this device, personify the opposing decisions or provide actors who 'hold the strings.' Anti-pattern: if there are no visible forces or agents to explain the manipulation, the effect will feel unmotivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Snow-ball / cumulative chain (arithmetical progression)
rubrics_metrics.description: A small cause sets off a chain reaction that grows progressively serious and unexpected (like a rolling snow-ball or a house of cards collapsing), culminating in an outsized result from an initially insignificant cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a causal chain where each step increases momentum or consequence (picture-book or comic-strip sequences are archetypal). The effect is strengthened by apparent inevitability and acceleration; variants include the 'vanishing important object' (a letter, hat) that continually eludes capture and 'rolls up' incidents through the play. Anti-pattern: if the chain lacks clear causal links or the escalation feels arbitrary, the comic effect diminishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversibility / circular return
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical combinations are often reversible or circular: efforts and incidents can return the plot to its starting point (the hero's long quest ends where he began), producing comic irony and the sense of effort for no result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use circular plotting (e.g., marriages/divorces bringing characters back together, the eaten hat returning as the sought hat) to produce the comic sense of wasted exertion. Note: Philosophical definitions (Spencer/Kant) describe laughter as expectation ending in nothing, but circularity alone is insufficient without the underlying mechanical image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of proportion is not the direct source
rubrics_metrics.description: Disproportion between cause and effect (great effect from small cause or vice versa) is not in itself the source of laughter; what matters is that this disproportion exposes an underlying mechanical arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing or constructing comic situations, seek the mechanical pattern that disproportion reveals. Merely striking imbalance without a visible mechanism or 'arrangement' will often fail to produce genuine comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic as absentmindedness / mechanisation of life
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic manifests where living continuity appears as rigid mechanism — movement without life — i.e., an individual or event reveals a likeness to a thing through inelasticity or automatism; laughter functions as a social corrective singling out this absentmindedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic scenes should make the audience perceive life’s lapse into mechanism (forgetfulness, rigidity, automatic behavior). Theorize scenes as exposing an 'absent-mindedness in things' and present them so the audience detects the foreign mechanical element in human affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal method: Repetition (situational)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition at the level of situation: a combination of circumstances recurs several times unchanged, contrasting with life’s continual change (examples: Molière’s plays reproducing the same incident in three tempi; masters and servants repeating analogous scenes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition is more laughable when the repeated scene is complex and appears naturally introduced; playwrights must reconcile complexity and naturalness. Contemporary comedies may prepare the audience for coincidences; classical comedy derives repetition organically from stable character 'forces.' Use symmetric or progressive recurrence across acts to build effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal method: Inversion (role reversal / topsyturvydom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invert the situation or roles (topsyturvydom): characters end up in reversed roles or are trapped by their own schemes (the 'robber robbed' or villain victim of his own villainy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inversion creates comic scenes when a trap recoils on its author (examples: Lawyer Pathelin, termagant wife with rota). Also, classical comic 'types' (robber robbed) can render otherwise non-comic mishaps comic by association—so referencing or echoing such types can trigger comic recognition. Anti-pattern: role reversal must be intelligible and motivated; inexplicable inversion feels contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal method: Reciprocal interference of independent series
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation becomes comic when it legitimately belongs simultaneously to two independent series of events and can be interpreted in two entirely different meanings (the stage-made misunderstanding/equivocal situation is one instance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes where separate lines of action or meaning meet so that actors only know one series while the audience perceives both. The comic derives from the revelation of independence + coincidence, and from repeated near-breakdowns patched up to restore the coincidence. Examples: equivocal stage misunderstandings, transposing past and present series (Tartarin manacled to Bonivard). Ensure the audience sees both series to reap the effect; mere equivocation without clear independent series may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-driven vs audience-driven acceptance of coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Two different dramaturgical strategies make repetition/coincidence acceptable: classical (repetition naturalized by characters’ constant forces) vs contemporary (preparing or 'mesmerising' the audience to accept coincidences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relying on character constancy (classic), make sure character motives independently produce repeated events; if relying on audience preparation (contemporary), gradually prime the audience so extraordinary coincidences feel admissible. Misusing strategy (forcing audience acceptance without preparation, or making characters act against established forces) undermines comic plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three archetypal contrasts with 'life' to generate comic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Life presents as irreversible time-evolution, evolving complexity in space, and unique closed systems; their opposites (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference) are the archetypal formal processes that generate comic situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting or analysing comedy, start from these three contrasts: introduce repetition (contradicting irreversibility), inversion (contradicting uniqueness/roles), or reciprocal interference (contradicting closed independent series). This provides a systematic method to discover 'every real and possible method of comedy.'
